explanation: When they sleep, glass frogs pack nearly all their red blood cells into their liver, which makes their bodies even harder for predators to see.

claims.text: Glass frogs have transparent belly skin through which their internal organs, including the beating heart, can be seen.
Poison dart frogs, horned frogs and leopard frogs do not have see-through bellies.
Sleeping glass frogs store nearly all of their red blood cells in the liver, which makes them more transparent.

evidence.restatement: Glass frogs (family Centrolenidae) have translucent belly skin through which the organs, often including the beating heart, can be seen.
Poison dart frogs, horned frogs and leopard frogs have opaque bellies.
When they sleep, glass frogs take most of their red blood cells (close to 90 percent) out of circulation and pack them into the liver, which makes them two to three times more transparent.

issues.note: The explanation says sleeping glass frogs pack 'nearly all' their red blood cells into the liver. The figure I know is close to 90 percent, so 'nearly 90 percent' or 'most' would be more exact. Not wrong at this precision.

evidence.restatement: Glass frogs have translucent belly skin, so the internal organs, heart included, can be seen.
Poison dart frogs, horned frogs and leopard frogs have opaque bellies.

Resting glass frogs hide most of their red blood cells in the liver, which makes the body more transparent. My recollection of the measured share is roughly nine in ten, which is 'most' or 'almost 90 per cent', not 'nearly all'.

claimResults.note: Mechanism recalled with confidence, magnitude not. 'Nearly all' looks stronger than the figure I remember. Not retrieved here: no search budget was available.

issues.note: c3 and the explanation say glass frogs pack 'nearly all' their red blood cells into the liver. The published share I recall is roughly 90 per cent at most, so 'nearly all' overstates it. Reword to 'most' (or 'about nine in ten') and have the figure confirmed externally.
The key 'Glass frogs' echoes 'see-through skin' in the stem, and no other option names a transparency. A cue rather than an error.

stem: Which rainforest frogs have see-through skin on their bellies, so you can watch their hearts beating?
